system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2175-10-02 19:15:00 to 2175-10-03 07:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: James, a man with a history of COPD, chronic pain, alcohol dependence, and tobacco use, was admitted after being found down and reporting a possible assault. He presented with alcohol intoxication and signs of withdrawal, including tremors, diaphoresis, and nausea. Trauma imaging showed no acute fractures or intracranial hemorrhage, though head CTs were limited by motion. He refused a repeat head CT due to radiation concerns. Treatment focused on alcohol withdrawal management with scheduled diazepam, IV fluids for volume depletion, and vitamin supplementation. His mental status improved, and withdrawal symptoms stabilized. Despite medical advice, he chose to leave against medical advice on the third day, declining further detoxification or rehab referral. He was discharged home with instructions to follow up and continue care.
problems: Chronic airway obstruction, not elsewhere classified
Contact dermatitis and other eczema, unspecified cause

diagnoses.long_title: Acute alcoholic intoxication in alcoholism, unspecified
Sedative, hypnotic or anxiolytic abuse, unspecified
Family history of malignant neoplasm of trachea, bronchus, and lung

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Patel. You're here because of a cough and being intoxicated. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had this cough for about a month. It’s worse now—yellow mucus, chest tightness. I can’t catch my breath well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned you’ve been drinking heavily. When was your last drink?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yesterday. I’ve been drunk for six months straight—quart of whiskey a day. I know it’s bad, but the pain in my face and leg won’t let up since that car hit me years ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. That must be really tough. We’re going to help you with that. First, your breathing—we’re giving you oxygen and some breathing treatments to help open your airways.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’m trying to do better. Last time I left the hospital early, but this time I want to stay. I think I need rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll get you started on treatment for your COPD flare-up and start medications to help with alcohol withdrawal, since you’re at risk for seizures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to go through withdrawal again. It’s awful. But I don’t want benzos—I’ve used them before. Can we do something else for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll manage your pain safely. Right now, you’re not in distress, and we’ll avoid opioids. We’re also restarting your blood pressure meds—you haven’t been taking them, have you?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I haven’t. My BP’s always high when I’m stressed or drinking. But I’m ready to change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big step. We’ve given you a breathing treatment, and your oxygen is helping. Your chest X-ray doesn’t show pneumonia, so we’re treating this as a COPD flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I need pain meds now. My face hurts. If you won’t give me something strong, I’m leaving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you’re in pain, but opioids aren’t safe right now, especially with your history. We can use acetaminophen and work on non-medication strategies. Please stay so we can help you safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t care. I want something that works. I’m done. I’m leaving now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I really urge you to stay. You’re at risk for severe alcohol withdrawal, even seizures. Your breathing is still unstable. Let’s find a way through this together.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. I’m going. I know my body. I’ll be fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m very concerned, but I respect your decision. We’ll discharge you against medical advice. Here are prescriptions to help—antibiotics, steroids for your lungs, blood pressure meds, and vitamins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fine. Just give me the scripts. I’ll follow up if I need to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please do. And consider calling the rehab center—we can refer you. Your health depends on it. Come back if you feel worse—shaking, confusion, trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll think about it. Thanks for trying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah. I’ll be okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve documented your discharge instructions. You’re alert and able to walk. Please don’t hesitate to return if things get worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’m heading out now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All right. Stay safe, and take those medications as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you.

summary.summary_paragraph: James, a man with a history of COPD, chronic pain from prior trauma, alcohol dependence, and tobacco use, was admitted for cough and alcohol intoxication. He initially expressed willingness to engage in treatment and rehab but became agitated and demanded opioid pain medication. When this was not provided due to safety concerns, he chose to leave against medical advice within an hour of admission. He did not receive treatment for COPD exacerbation or alcohol withdrawal, though breathing treatments provided some symptom relief. He was discharged alert and ambulatory with prescriptions for antibiotics, steroids, blood pressure medications, and vitamins, and urged to follow up and consider rehab. His chest X-ray showed no pneumonia, and blood cultures were negative.
